Bell's palsy

Controlled studies and pooled analyses generally report better short-term facial-function scores with PBM or laser acupuncture, although treatment settings and patient groups differ.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Controlled studies and pooled analyses generally report better short-term facial-function scores with PBM or laser acupuncture, although treatment settings and patient groups differ.

Summary of the Evidence

The direct Bell’s-palsy category contains 25 unique titles: 19 human primary reports, two systematic reviews, two meta-analyses, and two trial protocols. The human reports include five randomized trials, six other controlled or single-arm studies, six case reports, and two case series; they are not 19 independent trials. Two additional case reports concern broader peripheral facial palsy and are mapped as related evidence, not included in the direct count. Facial-nerve injury experiments in rats are also adjacent models rather than Bell’s-palsy studies.

Human and clinical evidence

A 2024 meta-analysis included 12 studies with 597 adults and pooled nine. Compared with control care, the pooled results favored laser treatment on House–Brackmann disease severity, Sunnybrook facial symmetry, and Facial Disability Index function scores (Lin et al. 2024). These estimates combine different treatment protocols and trial populations, so they summarize a range of interventions rather than one standardized dose.

In a randomized trial of 84 people whose Bell’s palsy had lasted more than eight weeks, laser acupuncture combined with PBM was compared with control care. At 12 weeks, fewer participants in the treatment group still had an abnormal House–Brackmann grade, and electrophysiological measures also favored treatment. The study is a single-center trial and tests PBM with laser acupuncture, not PBM alone (Wu et al. 2024).

A separate double-blind trial of 60 people tested multiwave laser treatment over six weeks and reported better facial-function outcomes than placebo (Alayat et al. 2022). The systematic reviews also describe some smaller trials with favorable findings and others without a clear group difference. Case reports and uncontrolled treatment series describe recovery, but spontaneous recovery and concurrent care make those changes difficult to attribute to light.

Animal evidence

No animal experiment in the exact Bell’s-palsy category directly models this idiopathic condition. Two rat facial-nerve injury studies are adjacent evidence on nerve repair; traumatic nerve injury is not the same disease process and those studies are not counted as Bell’s-palsy experiments.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone cell or ex-vivo study is classified in the direct Bell’s-palsy category.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Clinical records use near-infrared light around 808–905 nm, sometimes alongside 660 nm red visible light. Reported fluences in the review range are about 8–20 J/cm², with treatment periods commonly spanning six weeks; the 84-person late-stage trial used laser acupuncture points as well as PBM. Other trials apply light to facial muscles or nerve regions. Wavelength, dose, treatment site, disease stage, and added exercise or acupuncture vary. No head-to-head study establishes one preferred protocol.

Interpretation

Pooled facial-function scores and several controlled trials favor PBM or laser acupuncture over their comparators in the short term. The positive direction is seen across more than one outcome scale, while the evidence is less settled for durability and for attributing effects to PBM when it is combined with another intervention. Larger trials using a common protocol and longer follow-up would clarify those questions.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for short-term facial-function outcomes with PBM as an adjunct Low for durable recovery and less-studied patient groups
Publications and records25 unique titles in the direct category

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Several controlled studies and two pooled reviews report better facial-function scores after light treatment, including short-term results on House–Brackmann and Sunnybrook scales. The underlying trials remain small and use different wavelengths, treatment sites, and co-interventions. A larger blinded trial with a shared protocol and follow-up beyond treatment would show whether these score gains persist and apply across disease stages.
